label: Get the Job — Team Problem Solving
overview: The Get the Job — Team Problem Solving content gives advisors a complete facilitated team exercise system — covering two experiential exercises (Paper Tower and Spaghetti Tower), an analytical scoring model, a structured observational debrief, and a 9-step problem-solving framework to apply back at the workplace. The exercises create a high-pressure microcosm of the workplace, exposing real team dynamics in a safe environment. Advanced content suited to experienced advisors delivering off-site retreats, strategic planning days, or leadership development programs.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: What is the primary goal of this session — testing resource management and financial planning under pressure (Paper Tower), pure creativity and structural problem-solving (Spaghetti Tower), or teaching a structured problem-solving framework to a team that struggles to execute?

materials.name: Experiential Team-Building Task Sheets
materials.summary: Two ready-to-run exercises — the Paper Tower and the Spaghetti Tower — that test whether a team can plan and execute under pressure. Both impose hard limits: a fixed resource (paper in batches, or strictly 20 spaghetti sticks and a marshmallow) inside a rigid 30 minutes, 20 to prepare and 10 to build, with no prefabrication. The point is not the tower. It is a high-pressure microcosm of the workplace where dynamics, communication breakdowns and leadership styles surface in real time.
materials.who_when: Business owners, departmental managers and corporate teams at off-site retreats, strategic planning days or leadership training.
steps: Choose the exercise against your goal — Paper Tower for resource management and financial planning under pressure, Spaghetti Tower for pure creativity and structural problem-solving with brittle materials and a top-heavy constraint.
Distribute the task sheet and read the constraints aloud — 20 minutes to prepare, 10 to build, and prefabrication strictly forbidden.
Start the timer and do not intervene. Act as a silent observer for the full 30 minutes.
Document specific quotes and behaviours with exact timestamps — the moment a critical decision was made, and the moment the process broke down.
If running the Paper Tower, act as the supplier: hand out paper in batches of 20 and record their usage as you go.
When the build time expires, measure from the surface and confirm the tower stands unsupported for at least a minute.

materials.name: Paper Tower Model
materials.summary: The spreadsheet that turns the game into a financial exercise. It calculates a fictional profit or loss from materials drawn at $2,000 per batch of 20 sheets, the time taken, and the height achieved — with a $10,000 bonus above 2400mm. It shifts the goal from building the tallest tower to executing a profitable strategy, and it gives the advisor hard numbers to challenge the team with rather than impressions.
materials.who_when: Executive teams, project managers and finance departments who need to focus on resource allocation and profitability rather than sheer output.
steps: Record the materials the team draws as the exercise runs — every batch of 20 sheets costs them $2,000.
Record the time taken, in minutes.
Measure the final height once the tower has stood unsupported for a minute.
Enter materials, time and height into the model to produce their profit or loss, applying the $10,000 bonus if they cleared 2400mm.
Use the result in the debrief — the question that lands is whether anyone ran a financial calculation before they started building.

materials.name: Debrief & Process Frameworks
materials.summary: What turns a game into workplace change: a scripted observational debrief and the 9-step Core Problem Solving Process. Rather than generic questions, the advisor reads back exact time-stamped observations — "at 2:42 into the exercise, Jim said…" — and the deck's research-backed framing carries the authority. Teams fail these exercises for one recurring reason: they jump to solutions before they share an understanding of the problem.
materials.who_when: Any team suffering analysis paralysis, lacking structured meeting agendas, or struggling to carry ideas through to execution.
steps: Open the debrief by asking whether they enjoyed it, then move straight into reading back your time-stamped observations.
Ask the two questions that expose the gap: did anybody complete a financial calculation before developing the construction plan, and were you outcome-oriented or process-driven?
Move to the Team Problem Solving slides and explain the common failure — jumping to solutions without a shared understanding of the problem.
Walk the 9 steps, beginning with appointing a chairperson and a timekeeper.
Determine the objective (step 3) — written, and S.M.A.R.T.: specific, measurable, agreed, revisable and time-bound. It must state not just what is being done but why it matters.
Brainstorm without assessment (step 5) — judgment deferred entirely. Congratulate every contribution to hold psychological safety and keep the thinking divergent.
Eliminate and select the best option (step 7) — move to convergent thinking, using an Impact versus Effort matrix to narrow to the high-impact solutions.
Allocate resources and build the action plan (steps 8 and 9) — a solution without a budget or a team is only a wish.
Appoint an Enforcer to take psychological and operational ownership: monitoring milestones, reporting progress and barriers, and keeping the momentum from dissipating.
Close by brainstorming where this 9-step process applies back at work, so the session earns its return.

advisor_guidance.observer_discipline: The advisor's job during the exercise is silent observation — not facilitation. Resist the urge to help, guide, or encourage. Every moment of struggle you allow to play out becomes evidence for a more powerful debrief.
advisor_guidance.debrief_specificity: Generic debrief questions produce generic answers. Time-stamped observations make the debrief specific and credible. 'At 2:42, Jim said...' is worth more than 'I noticed the group struggled to communicate.'
advisor_guidance.enforce_brainstorming_rule: The single most important rule in the 9-Step Framework is: no assessment during brainstorming. Enforce it without exception. Premature assessment kills divergent thinking and reduces the quality of the final solution.

if_then_logic.condition: The client wants to test resource management and financial planning under pressure
if_then_logic.action: Select and distribute the Paper Tower Task Sheet. Use the Paper Tower Model spreadsheet to calculate the profit or loss result after the build.
if_then_logic.context: The Paper Tower exercise forces the team to balance material cost ($2,000 per batch) against revenue (height) to achieve profitability — connecting the exercise directly to financial planning.

if_then_logic.condition: The client wants a pure creativity and structural problem-solving challenge without the financial dimension
if_then_logic.action: Select and distribute the Spaghetti Tower Task Sheet.
if_then_logic.context: The Spaghetti Tower focuses purely on height and structural integrity using highly brittle materials (spaghetti) and a top-heavy constraint (marshmallow). No financial model required.

if_then_logic.condition: The 30-minute exercise concludes and the towers are measured
if_then_logic.action: Transition immediately to the Paper Tower Review Questions. Open with 'Did you have fun?', then read back time-stamped observations from your notes.
if_then_logic.context: State exactly what you saw and heard. Ask if they were outcome-oriented or process-driven. The debrief must follow the exercise directly while the experience is still fresh.

if_then_logic.condition: The team failed the exercise because they immediately started building without a plan
if_then_logic.action: Present Step 3 of the Team Problem Solving deck: 'Determine the Objective.' Explain that the most common failure is jumping to solutions without a S.M.A.R.T. objective.
if_then_logic.context: A S.M.A.R.T. objective must state not only what is being done, but why it is important. Teams that skip this step cannot evaluate whether their solution is working.

if_then_logic.condition: Team members are arguing or shooting down each other's ideas during the brainstorming phase of the 9-step framework
if_then_logic.action: Enforce Step 5: Brainstorm Without Assessment. Remind the team that judgment must be deferred entirely. Congratulate all contributions.
if_then_logic.context: Premature assessment is the most frequent failure point in brainstorming. Psychological safety must be enforced by the facilitator — it will not emerge naturally under pressure.

if_then_logic.condition: The team has selected a great idea but has a history of failing to implement
if_then_logic.action: Enforce Steps 8 and 9: allocate resources and appoint an Enforcer who takes operational ownership of the Action Plan.
if_then_logic.context: A solution without a budget or a dedicated owner is merely a wish. The Enforcer monitors milestones and reports back — ensuring the ROI of the session is realised.
